nodes.name: Theodor Herzl
nodes.note: Theodor Herzl — assimilated Viennese Jew, secular by outlook, correspondent for Neue Freie Presse — wrote Der Judenstaat (1896) and convened the First Zionist Congress in Basel Aug 29-31 1897. His own words in his diary after Basel: 'At Basel I founded the Jewish State.' Founded — his word. The idea was older: from the 1840s the Sephardi rabbi Yehuda Alkalai urged settlement in the land, and from 1882 the Hovevei Zion societies organized it  ; what Basel created was the organized, international political movement. Full scene at [4]. Herzl considered Argentina and Uganda as candidate territories before Palestine was settled on. Political Zionism at founding was territorially agnostic. That is How his work was paid for: he founded Die Welt at his own expense (1897); the movement's own money came from shekel dues and the Jewish Colonial Trust's share sale to over 100,000 small subscribers (1899). Baron de Hirsch, Albert Rothschild of Vienna and Edmond de Rothschild of Paris did not fund his political plan.

nodes.name: Ahad Ha'am
nodes.note: Asher Zvi Hirsch Ginsberg — 'Ahad Ha'am' (One of the People), 1856-1927. Argued for cultural Zionism — a Jewish spiritual and cultural center in Palestine — while explicitly warning against political Zionism as Herzl framed it. His 1891 essay 'Truth from Eretz Israel' documented Palestinian Arab presence and warned Herzl's project would produce conflict. Jewish. Zionist in the cultural sense. Explicitly opposed to the political Zionism that became the state. On record from the founding decade.

nodes.name: Leon Pinsker
nodes.note: Jews had their own name for it. In 1882, after pogroms in the Russian Empire, the Odessa physician Leon Pinsker published 'Auto-Emancipation,' which called the hatred 'Judeophobia': an irrational fear of Jews that he described as an inherited disease. The name says plainly who the target is. Pinsker concluded that Jews needed a homeland of their own, which makes the pamphlet one of the founding texts of Zionism.

nodes.name: Moses Hess
nodes.note: German socialist philosopher, early collaborator of Marx. His 1862 book "Rome and Jerusalem" was one of the earliest arguments for Jewish national return — read by very few at the time. The book proposed a Jewish state in Palestine as a socialist project. Hess died in 1875 largely unread. The 1897 Zionist Congress [scene 4] would rediscover him as a founding intellectual figure two decades after his death. This is the pattern: Zionism as a modern political idea has specific 19th-century intellectual roots.
